label: Out of Scope
oneLiner: Introduces a topic, group, or issue the stimulus never addresses.
definition: Out-of-scope answers can be true and interesting, but they do not bear on the task.

examples.text: Stimulus about advisory opinions; answer about whether they should be binding.

keyPoints.point: Introduces a topic, group, or issue the stimulus never addresses.

card.front: An answer discusses a group the stimulus never mentions. Trap?

label: Too Strong
definition: Fatal on inference and NA questions; acceptable on SA questions.

card.back: Sufficient Assumption (and sometimes Strengthen/Weaken); never in Must Be True or Necessary Assumption.

label: Reversal
definition: From A → B, the answer asserts B → A.

examples.text: Stimulus: clause → bypass; answer: bypass → clause.

card.front: Stimulus: A → B. Answer: B → A. Trap?

label: Half-Right / Half-Wrong
oneLiner: One part fits; another part fails.
definition: Common in two-part Role, Method, and dialogue answers.

examples.text: Point at Issue answer that only one speaker addresses.

keyPoints.point: One part fits; another part fails.

card.front: How do you beat half-right answers?
card.back: Check every clause of the answer against the stimulus.

label: Irrelevant Comparison
oneLiner: Compares things the argument does not need to compare.
definition: Typically “more than” / “less than” statements about outside groups.

examples.text: Stimulus about one fund; answer comparing other funds’ fees.

keyPoints.point: Compares things the argument does not need to compare.

card.front: An answer compares the subject to an outside group. Usual trap?

label: Opposite
oneLiner: Does the reverse of the task (weakens on a strengthen question).
definition: Especially dangerous under time pressure and EXCEPT questions.

examples.text: Strengthen question; answer supplies an alternative cause.

keyPoints.point: Does the reverse of the task (weakens on a strengthen question).

label: Shell Game
oneLiner: Swaps a key term for a similar-sounding one.
definition: The answer uses the stimulus’s vocabulary but changes the concept (citations → influence; length → quality).

keyPoints.point: Swaps a key term for a similar-sounding one.

card.front: “More citations” in the stimulus becomes “more influence” in the answer. Trap?

label: Unsupported Inference
oneLiner: Could be true, but the stimulus does not establish it.
definition: Fatal on Must Be True; wrong on Cannot Be True too (possible ≠ impossible).

examples.text: Nothing about pre-2010 treaties; answer asserts something about them.

keyPoints.point: Could be true, but the stimulus does not establish it.

card.front: Is an unsupported answer correct on Cannot Be True?
card.back: No—unsupported claims could still be true.

label: Wrong Degree
oneLiner: Right direction, wrong strength (some vs. most; weakens slightly).

examples.text: “Some firms will pay dividends” vs. “most firms pay no tax.”

keyPoints.point: Right direction, wrong strength (some vs. most; weakens slightly).

card.front: Two answers weaken; one says “some”, one breaks the mechanism for most. Which wins?
card.back: The broader one—“some” is Wrong Degree.

label: Restatement of Premise
oneLiner: Repeats a premise; useless on assumption, strengthen, and flaw questions.
definition: Premises are already given; repeating them adds nothing.

examples.text: NA answer that simply repeats the stimulus’s second sentence.

keyPoints.point: Repeats a premise; useless on assumption, strengthen, and flaw questions.

card.front: Why is restating a premise wrong on Necessary Assumption?
card.back: Assumptions are unstated; a premise is already stated.
